drills.q: Whiteboard ECDSA sign+verify over secp256k1 from memory, then identify the single step whose failure compromises the key.
drills.a: Sign: z=H(m); R=kG; r=x_R mod n; s=k^-1(z+r d) mod n. Verify: w=s^-1; X=zwG+rwQ; check x_X==r mod n. Failure point: nonce k generation - reuse leaks d via k=(z1-z2)(s1-s2)^-1.

drills.q: Compute the Merkle proof size for a block with 4096 transactions and state how many hashes verification costs.
drills.a: log2(4096)=12 levels; proof = 12 sibling hashes = 384 bytes; verification = 12 SHA-256 compressions. Root stored in the 80-byte header commits to all txs.

drills.q: An attacker shows you two documents with identical MD5. Which hash property failed and roughly how much work was that in 2012 vs today?
drills.a: Collision resistance. Chosen-prefix MD5 collisions were practical from ~2008 (rogue CA 2008-2012 era, minutes-to-hours on clusters). For SHA-256 the same attack is ~2^128 - infeasible.

drills.q: Your API authenticates requests with SHA256(secret_key || body). What breaks and what do you ship instead?
drills.a: Length extension: digest reveals internal state so suffixes can be appended and re-hashed without the key. Ship HMAC-SHA256 (nested keyed construction) or truncate-with-care alternatives like KMAC/SipHash.

drills.q: Implement RFC 6979 in one paragraph: inputs, primitive, loop structure.
drills.a: Inputs: private scalar x (32-byte BE) and digest h1 reduced mod n. V=0x01*32, K=0x00*32; K=HMAC(K,V||0x00||x||h1); V=HMAC(K,V); K=HMAC(K,V||0x01||x||h1); V=HMAC(K,V); loop: V=HMAC(K,V); candidate=int(V); if 1<=candidate<n use it else K=HMAC(K,V||0x00), V=HMAC(K,V). Deterministic k from (key,message): RNG failures stop being catastrophic.

drills.q: A mempool watcher reports your confirmed transaction's hash changing while sender/signature stay constant. Diagnose.
drills.a: Signature malleability: attacker rebroadcast (r, n-s) which verifies identically but has a different txid. Fix at protocol level: low-s enforcement (EIP-2, BIP-62); at app level track by intent (nonce/sender) not raw txid.

drills.q: Design tamper-evidence for a 500 GB audit log where auditors occasionally challenge one record. Full blockchain, or something else?
drills.a: Merkle tree over log chunks + externally anchored root (CT-log style or periodic chain anchoring). Challenge served as a 25-hash branch (~800 bytes). Running a blockchain adds consensus you don't need - one honest party holding roots plus append-only storage suffices.

drills.q: Explain why a naive binary Merkle tree without leaf/node prefixes admits a forged proof, concretely.
drills.a: Internal node value H(A||B) is just bytes; craft a fake 'leaf' whose content equals those bytes. Now present the shorter proof path for the fake leaf - verifier cannot distinguish leaf-level from node-level hashing without domain separation (RFC 6962 prefixes 0x00/0x01).

drills.q: Your team wants BLS aggregation everywhere. Give two reasons to push back.
drills.a: Verification is ~5-10x ECDSA cost per signature, hurting high-throughput single-sig paths; aggregation needs distinct-message discipline or proofs-of-possession to prevent rogue-key attacks; ecosystem/hardware support is ECDSA-centric. Use BLS where aggregation pays (consensus committees), not universally.

drills.q: Quantum adversary timeline: rank primitives here by urgency and justify with numbers.
drills.a: 1) ECDSA/Schnorr/BLS keys: Shor breaks them in poly time - existential. 2) SHA-256: Grover halves exponent, preimage ~2^128 - safe indefinitely for practical purposes. Migration pain: ML-DSA sigs ~2.4-4.6 KB vs 64 B; lost keys (dead wallets) cannot be rotated, so quantum raid of unmovable coins remains unsolved.

drills.q: A junior engineer proposes storing private keys as environment variables and signing directly in application code 'since we control the servers.' What's your response?
drills.a: The primitives can be sound while key custody is the actual failure point -- an env-var key is readable by anything with process access, has no audit trail, and if leaked compromises every past and future signature permanently with no rotation equivalent. Use a signing service or HSM that performs signing internally and never exports the private key; the app only ever receives (r, s).

drills.q: Does using an HSM fully eliminate ECDSA nonce-reuse risk?
drills.a: No. An HSM protects key material from exfiltration, but if its internal nonce generation is buggy or non-RFC-6979-compliant, nonce reuse is still possible in principle. Verify via vendor documentation or independent audit that the HSM's ECDSA implementation uses deterministic or properly-audited random nonce generation -- don't assume 'hardware' implies immunity to this specific algebraic attack.
